questions.title: Key phrase for CPR chest compression quality
questions.question: The "key phrase" for chest compression in CPR is:

options.A: Push at a rate of 30 compressions per minute
options.B: Check the pulse after each compression.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The compression rate taught is at least 100 per minute, not 30 per minute; 30 is instead the number of compressions given per cycle of 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths in single-rescuer CPR, a different number for a different purpose.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pulse is not checked between individual compressions during CPR; doing so would interrupt the compressions that generate circulation and delay restarting them.
explanations.C: Correct. "Push hard and fast" is the key phrase summarising the two targets that matter most for compression quality: adequate depth, roughly two inches (5cm) in an adult, and adequate rate, at least 100 per minute, with full chest recoil between compressions. Compressions that are too shallow or too slow fail to generate enough forward blood flow to perfuse the brain and heart during cardiac arrest. This mnemonic is taught precisely because it is easy to remember and apply correctly under the pressure of a real resuscitation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Five inches is far deeper than the roughly two-inch (5cm) depth taught for adult chest compressions; a compression this deep would risk rib or sternal fracture without added benefit.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: State that "push hard and fast" is the key phrase summarising CPR's adequate-depth and adequate-rate compression targets.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > CPR compression quality

questions.title: Pulse-check landmark for an unconscious child
questions.question: In an unconscious CHILD check the pulse by using two fingers to feel:

explanations.A: Correct. This paper's own key teaches checking an unconscious child's pulse at the brachial artery, felt at the medial side of the antecubital fossa, using two fingers. Some resuscitation curricula reserve the brachial pulse specifically for an infant under one year and use the carotid or femoral pulse for an older child, so this course's use of "child" for the brachial landmark may extend the term loosely to include infants; the marked key is followed here as this course's own taught convention.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The femoral artery, in the groin, is an alternative central-pulse site taught in some curricula, but it is not the site this paper's own key marks for an unconscious child.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The carotid artery, in the neck, is the classic adult and older-child pulse-check site in many BLS courses, but it is not the site this paper's own key marks here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "The heart" is not a peripheral pulse-check site at all; a pulse is felt at an artery, not by attempting to feel the heart directly through the chest wall.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: State the pulse-check landmark this paper's key teaches for an unconscious child: the brachial artery, checked with two fingers.

questions.title: Signs of severe upper airway obstruction in an adult
questions.question: Adult patient with severe upper airway obstruction may present by all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is true, so it is not the answer to an EXCEPT question). Inability to breathe or speak is the classic presentation of severe, near-complete or complete upper airway obstruction, since air can no longer move past the obstruction to produce speech or adequate ventilation.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement is true). If severe obstruction is not relieved, hypoxia develops, producing cyanosis and a falling conscious level as recognised, worsening signs of ongoing obstruction.
explanations.C: Correct. Hypotension and vomiting are not recognised signs of severe upper airway obstruction; they belong instead to other conditions such as shock or a gastrointestinal problem. The recognised signs of choking are difficulty breathing or speaking, coughing, the universal choking sign of clutching the throat, cyanosis and falling consciousness if the obstruction persists, none of which is hypotension or vomiting, which is what makes this statement false and therefore the answer to this EXCEPT question.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is true). Wheezy breath sounds can occur with partial upper airway obstruction as air is forced past a narrowed passage, so this is a recognised finding, not the false statement being asked for.

questions.learning_objective: List the recognised signs of severe upper airway obstruction and distinguish them from unrelated findings such as hypotension and vomiting.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Recognising choking

questions.title: First step in adult choking management
questions.question: In management of severe upper airway obstruction (choking) in adult patient begin with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Abdominal thrusts are the second step, attempted only if five back blows fail to clear the obstruction, not the first step.
explanations.B: Correct. Management of severe choking in an adult begins with five sharp back blows between the shoulder blades; only if these fail does the rescuer move on to five abdominal thrusts, alternating the two in cycles of five if the obstruction persists. This back-blows-first sequence is what this paper's own course teaches, and reflects the same principle followed by several international resuscitation councils.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CPR is started only if the choking patient becomes unresponsive, not as the first step while the patient is still conscious and obstructed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An AED is used for cardiac arrest, not as an initial step in managing a conscious choking patient.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: Sequence adult choking management, stating that five back blows are attempted before abdominal thrusts.

questions.title: How to check breathing in an unconscious patient
questions.question: To check breathing in an unconscious patient, all of the followings are right EXCEPT:

options.B: Hearing sounds comes out from airway.
options.C: Feeling air coming out from the nose or mouth

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is true). Observing chest-wall movement, the "look" step, is one of the three components of the bedside breathing check.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement is true). Listening for breath sounds at the mouth and nose, the "listen" step, is another of the three components of the bedside breathing check.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement is true). Feeling for exhaled air against the cheek, the "feel" step, completes the look/listen/feel breathing check.
explanations.D: Correct. Doing a chest X-ray plays no role in the immediate bedside breathing check: it is neither available nor fast enough during the roughly ten-second assessment that decides whether to start CPR, unlike the look, listen and feel steps, which use only the rescuer's own senses. This makes the X-ray statement false, which is what an EXCEPT question is asking for.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: State that breathing is assessed by looking, listening and feeling, not by imaging.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Breathing check technique

questions.title: Correct chest-compression hand position during CPR
questions.question: Regarding chest compression on doing CPR, all of the followings are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: Compression should be for two inches.
options.B: Put the heel of hands on the upper abdomen.
options.C: Allow the chest to recoil completely.
options.D: The compression rate should be at least 100/min.

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is true). Roughly two inches (5cm) is the target compression depth for an adult, so this statement is correct and not the answer to this EXCEPT question.
explanations.B: Correct. Chest compressions are placed with the heel of the hand over the lower half of the sternum, not the upper abdomen; the upper abdomen is instead the landmark for the different technique of an abdominal thrust used in choking, as this paper's own handwritten margin note ("→ choking") on this item points out. Placing compression hands on the upper abdomen would not compress the heart at all and risks injuring abdominal organs such as the liver, which is why this statement is false and is the answer to this EXCEPT question.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement is true). Allowing full chest recoil between compressions lets the heart refill with blood before the next compression, so this statement is correct.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is true). At least 100 compressions per minute is the target rate, so this statement is correct and not the answer being asked for.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: State that chest-compression hand placement is the lower half of the sternum, not the upper abdomen.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > CPR compression technique

questions.title: Correct hand position for a choking abdominal thrust
questions.question: When performing a choking abdominal thrust, which is the correct area to place your hand fist?

options.B: On the back of the chest

explanations.A: Incorrect. Placing the fist over the sternum describes chest-compression hand position for CPR, not the abdominal-thrust technique for choking.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The back of the chest is the site for back blows, a different choking technique, not for an abdominal thrust.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lower abdomen is too low a landmark; thrusts delivered there are less effective and risk injury to lower abdominal or pelvic structures.
explanations.D: Correct. The abdominal thrust (Heimlich manoeuvre) is delivered with a fist placed on the upper abdomen, in the midline between the umbilicus and the tip of the sternum, with sharp inward-and-upward thrusts. This location generates a sudden rise in intra-abdominal and intrathoracic pressure that can expel the obstructing object, which is why this specific landmark, rather than the sternum, back or lower abdomen, is the one taught for this technique.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: State the correct fist placement for an abdominal thrust: the upper abdomen, between the umbilicus and the tip of the sternum.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Abdominal thrust technique

questions.title: Managing a choking infant
questions.question: For an INFANT who is choking, you would perform….

options.D: Hold the infant upside down and strike between the shoulder blades.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The Heimlich (abdominal thrust) manoeuvre is contraindicated in an infant, because an infant's relatively large, poorly protected liver is at risk of injury from the pressure an abdominal thrust generates.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CPR is reserved for a choking infant who becomes unresponsive, not used as the first-line technique while the infant is still responsive and obstructed.
explanations.C: Correct. A choking infant under one year is managed with alternating back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts, because of the injury risk abdominal thrusts pose to an infant's abdominal organs. This substitution of chest thrusts for abdominal thrusts is the specific, age-appropriate technique this paper's key teaches for an infant.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Holding the infant upside down by the ankles and striking the back is an outdated, unsafe practice, not the recommended technique; correct back blows are delivered with the infant prone along the rescuer's forearm, head-down, not held upside down by the ankles.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: State that infant choking is managed with back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts, CPR, or holding the infant upside down.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Infant choking management

questions.title: Safety precautions during AED shock delivery
questions.question: Regarding Automated External Defibrillator (AED), all of the followings are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: Do rescue breathing during the electric shock.
options.B: AED restore the heart into a normal perfusing rhythm.
options.C: Continue CPR while AED is being attached.
options.D: Stand away and do not touch the patient before starting the shock.

explanations.A: Correct. Rescue breathing is never given during the shock itself: giving it would mean touching the patient's airway at the exact moment nobody should be in contact with them, and CPR (including rescue breaths) is deliberately paused for the shock and resumed immediately afterwards rather than given through it. This makes the statement false, which is what an EXCEPT question is asking for.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement is true). Restoring the heart to a normal, perfusing rhythm is the purpose of the shock an AED delivers, so this statement is correct.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement is true). CPR is continued while the AED is being attached and is analysing the rhythm, right up until a shock is advised and about to be delivered, so this statement is correct.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this statement is true). Everyone must stand clear and not touch the patient before the shock is delivered, since the current can pass through anyone in contact with the patient, so this statement is correct.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: State that rescuers must stand clear of the patient during an AED shock and that rescue breathing is not given during the shock, while CPR continues up to the point the shock is delivered.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > AED shock safety

questions.title: What polytrauma management includes
questions.question: Management of polytraumatized patient includes all the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this statement is true). Primary survey performed simultaneously with resuscitation, treating life-threatening problems as they are found, is the first stage of polytrauma management.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this statement is true). Secondary survey and targeted investigations follow once the patient is stabilised, so this statement correctly describes the second stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this statement is true). Definitive treatment of the injuries identified is the final stage of this sequence, so this statement is correct.
explanations.D: Correct. Early oral feeding is not a recognised part of acute polytrauma management: a trauma patient's airway, level of consciousness and gastrointestinal function cannot be assumed safe for oral intake in the acute phase, and unnecessary oral intake before injuries are fully assessed risks aspiration and can complicate any surgery that follows. This makes the statement false, which is what an EXCEPT question is asking for.

questions.learning_objective: State the correct sequence for polytrauma management (primary survey with resuscitation, secondary survey and investigations, definitive treatment) and that early oral feeding is not part of it.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Polytrauma management

questions.title: Transporting a patient with suspected cervical spine injury
questions.question: Trauma patient with suspected cervical spine injury should transported.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sitting the patient in a wheelchair does not immobilise the cervical spine and allows movement that could worsen an unstable injury.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A strong analgesic injection treats pain but does not stabilise the spine, and could mask worsening pain that would otherwise signal a deteriorating injury.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fully extending the neck is exactly the kind of movement cervical spine precautions are meant to avoid in a patient with a suspected unstable injury.
explanations.D: Correct. A trauma patient with suspected cervical spine injury is transported with the neck immobilised by a properly fitted cervical collar, often combined with head blocks and a spinal board, to prevent movement of an unstable spine that could cause or worsen spinal cord injury. None of sitting, analgesia, or neck extension provides this mechanical stabilisation, which is why fixation with a collar is the correct method of transport.

questions.learning_objective: State that suspected cervical spine injury is managed by transporting the patient with the neck immobilised in a cervical collar, not sitting, with the neck extended, or after analgesic injection alone.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Cervical spine precautions

questions.title: What the Glasgow Coma Scale measures
questions.question: Glasgow coma scale (GCS) is used to measure.

explanations.A: Correct. The Glasgow Coma Scale is a standardised scoring tool used to measure and communicate a patient's level of consciousness, combining eye-opening, verbal and motor responses into a single reproducible score. It is a distinct tool from those used to grade other trauma domains, which is why the remaining options each describe a different clinical assessment altogether.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Haemorrhagic shock is graded by its own classification (based on findings such as heart rate, blood pressure and blood loss), not by the GCS.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Airway obstruction is assessed by its own signs (such as stridor, gurgling or inability to speak), not by the GCS.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bone fracture is assessed by clinical examination and imaging, not by the GCS, which addresses consciousness rather than the skeleton.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Glasgow Coma Scale is used to measure level of consciousness, not haemorrhagic shock, airway obstruction, or fracture severity.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Glasgow Coma Scale

questions.title: Definition of the definitive airway
questions.question: The definitive airway is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. An oropharyngeal tube is a basic airway adjunct that helps keep the airway patent, but it does not seal the trachea and so is not a definitive airway.
explanations.B: Correct. A "definitive airway" is a cuffed tube placed within the trachea, most often by orotracheal (orolaryngeal) intubation, which secures the airway against aspiration and allows controlled or assisted ventilation. Because it seals the trachea itself, it is categorically different from adjuncts or non-invasive ventilation methods, which only support the existing, unsealed airway.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Face-mask breathing is a non-invasive ventilation method; it delivers breaths but does not secure or seal the airway, so it is not a definitive airway.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rescue mouth breathing is likewise a non-invasive method of delivering breaths, not a means of securing the trachea, so it is not a definitive airway either.

questions.learning_objective: State that the definitive airway is orotracheal/orolaryngeal intubation, distinguishing it from basic adjuncts (oropharyngeal tube) and non-invasive ventilation methods (face mask or mouth breathing).
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Definitive airway

questions.title: What the trauma primary survey includes
questions.question: Primary survey for management of traumatized patient includes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. X-rays for fracture belong to the secondary survey and later investigation, once the primary survey has confirmed the patient is not in immediate danger, not to the primary survey itself.
explanations.B: Correct. The primary survey for a traumatized patient is structured around the ABCDE sequence, airway with cervical spine control, breathing, circulation with haemorrhage control, disability, exposure, assessing and treating immediately life-threatening problems in that fixed order. This is what distinguishes the primary survey from the secondary survey and later investigations, which address less urgent findings only after ABCDE has confirmed the patient is stable enough to proceed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Blood tests such as an anaemia screen are part of the secondary survey's investigations, not the primary survey.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prophylactic IV antibiotics are part of later management once the patient is stabilised and injuries assessed, not a primary-survey step.

questions.learning_objective: State that a trauma patient's primary survey follows the ABCDE guidelines, distinguishing this from secondary-survey investigations such as X-rays, blood tests, or antibiotics.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Primary survey (ABCDE)

questions.title: Requirements for transferring a polytraumatized patient
questions.question: Transfer of polytraumatized patients should include:

options.B: One or two appropriately sized IV lines.
options.C: Cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry is initiated.

explanations.A: Incorrect (this option alone is incomplete). A secure airway is one necessary requirement, but transfer requires this together with IV access and monitoring, not this alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this option alone is incomplete). IV access is another necessary requirement, but it does not by itself cover the airway or monitoring needs of a safe transfer.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this option alone is incomplete). Cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring is a third necessary requirement, but airway security and IV access are still needed alongside it.
explanations.D: Correct. Before and during transfer of a polytraumatized patient, the airway must already be secured, one or two appropriately sized IV lines should be in place, and continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring should be running, so the patient's status can be tracked and any deterioration acted on throughout the transfer. All three are required together, each protecting against a different way the patient could deteriorate in transit, which is why "all the above" rather than any single option is correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that safe transfer of a polytraumatized patient requires a secured airway, IV access, and cardiac/pulse-oximetry monitoring together, not any one alone.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Polytrauma transfer

questions.title: Managing choking in an infant under one year
questions.question: In management of upper airway obstruction (choking) in an infant less than one year:

options.A: Keep the head up to open the airway.
options.C: Starts with 5 back thrust while the baby is prone with head downwards

explanations.A: Incorrect. Keeping the head up is the opposite of the head-down positioning actually used during infant back blows; head-up positioning does not use gravity to help dislodge the obstructing object.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Abdominal thrusts are contraindicated in an infant because of the risk of injury to the infant's relatively large, poorly protected liver, so management never starts with abdominal thrusts in this age group.
explanations.C: Correct. Management of choking in an infant under one year starts with five back blows, delivered with the infant held prone along the rescuer's forearm, head lower than the trunk, using the heel of the hand between the shoulder blades. This head-down, prone positioning uses gravity to help dislodge the obstructing object, and is the specific technique this paper's key teaches as the first step, rather than abdominal thrusts or CPR.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CPR is reserved for a choking infant who becomes unresponsive, not used as the first step in a still-responsive, obstructed infant.

questions.topic: Basic life support and airway management
questions.learning_objective: State that infant choking management starts with five back blows delivered with the infant prone and head-down, not with abdominal thrusts or CPR as a first step.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-108 > Professional Practice II > Infant choking technique
